stem: In a total trade receivables account, credit sales are:

options.content: the balancing figure, entered on the debit side
options.rationale: Correct: sales on credit increase receivables, which is a debit.

options.content: the balancing figure, entered on the credit side
options.rationale: Credit sales increase the receivables balance, so they are debited.

options.content: a figure always taken from the bank statement
options.rationale: The bank statement shows cash received, not credit sales.

options.content: the closing balance of the account
options.rationale: The closing balance is what customers still owe.

explanation: Opening receivables and credit sales go on the debit side; cash received, discounts, returns and write-offs and the closing balance go on the credit side.

stem: A trader adds 50% to the cost of every item sold. What is the gross profit margin?

options.rationale: 50% is the mark-up on cost, not the margin on sales.
50 is a third of the selling price of 150, not a quarter.
That would be 100 ÷ 150, a figure unrelated to the gross profit.

explanation: Cost 100, selling price 150, gross profit 50. Margin = 50 ÷ 150 = 33⅓%.
hints: Take cost as 100 and find the selling price.

stem: A summary of a business bank statement shows all payments except one cash withdrawal. The balancing figure is treated as the owner's:

options.rationale: Capital introduced would be a receipt, not a payment.
Credit sales are not a bank payment.
Depreciation is not a cash movement.
Correct: money taken out and not otherwise explained.

explanation: When every other payment is known, the unexplained payment is drawings.

stem: Trade payables were US\$3,740 at the start and US\$4,215 at the end of the year. Payments to suppliers were US\$26,880, discount received US\$330 and returns outwards US\$560. Calculate credit purchases for the year.

options.rationale: The change in the payables balance has been ignored.
Correct: closing balance plus payments, discount and returns, less the opening balance.
Discount received and returns outwards were left out.
The opening and closing balances have been reversed.

hints: Draw the account: credit purchases are the balancing figure on the credit side.

stem: Cash sales of US\$5,740 and credit sales of US\$38,190 are known. Returns inwards were US\$860. What is the revenue?

options.rationale: Returns inwards have not been deducted.
Correct: total sales of 43,930 less returns inwards.
Cash sales have been left out.
Returns inwards have been added.

stem: Revenue was US\$74,400 and the business adds a mark-up of 20% on cost. What was the cost of sales?

options.rationale: 20% of sales has been deducted, which uses the margin, not the mark-up.
The mark-up has been added to revenue instead of removed.
This is the 20% itself, not the cost.

stem: Inventory lost in a fire is estimated using the usual gross profit margin. Which is the key assumption?

options.content: All of the inventory in the stock room was destroyed
options.rationale: Salvage is deducted; the method does not assume total loss.

options.content: Purchases were all paid for in cash
options.rationale: The method uses purchases whether paid or not.

options.content: The margin earned before the fire was the same as the usual margin
options.rationale: Correct: otherwise the cost of sales, and hence the inventory, is wrong.
The method exists to find the closing inventory.

explanation: Cost of sales is calculated from sales and the margin, so the result depends on the margin being the same during the period.
hints: The cost of sales is derived from the margin.

stem: In a total receivables account, irrecoverable debts written off of US\$420 were left out. What is the effect on credit sales found as the balancing figure?

options.content: Credit sales are overstated by US\$420
options.rationale: Leaving out a credit item lowers the balancing debit.
Every item in the account affects the balance.

options.content: Credit sales are understated by US\$840
options.rationale: The error is 420 once, not twice.

options.content: Credit sales are understated by US\$420
options.rationale: Correct: the credit side is too small, so the balancing figure on the debit side is too small.

explanation: A missing credit entry makes the credit side smaller and the balancing debit (credit sales) smaller by the same amount.
hints: Which side is each item on?

stem: A gross profit margin of 20% is the same as a mark-up of 20%.
explanation: False. A 20% margin equals a 25% mark-up, because 20 of profit on 100 of sales is 20 on cost of 80.

stem: A cash-in-hand summary can show cash stolen as a balancing figure only if every other receipt and payment is known.
explanation: True. It absorbs any unrecorded item, so the claim of theft needs complete other information.
hints: The balancing figure absorbs any unrecorded item.

stem: Match each item to the side of the total trade receivables account on which it appears.

left.content: Balance at the start of the year

explanation: Opening balance and credit sales are debits; cash received, discount allowed, returns inwards, write-offs and the closing balance are credits.

stem: Complete the definitions.

payload.template: Mark-up is gross profit as a percentage of {{blank:a}}; gross profit margin is gross profit as a percentage of {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Mark-up uses cost of sales as its base; margin uses revenue.

stem: What name is given to the figure that makes the two sides of a summary account equal?
explanation: The balancing figure is the unknown total that completes the account.

stem: Trade receivables were US\$4,275 at 1 January and US\$5,130 at 31 December. Customers paid US\$36,940. Discount allowed was US\$615, returns inwards US\$1,185 and irrecoverable debts written off US\$395. Calculate the credit sales for the year.
explanation: Credit sales = 5,130 + 36,940 + 615 + 1,185 + 395 - 4,275 = 39,990. Ignoring the balances gives 39,135.
workedSolution: 1. Credit sales = 5,130 + 36,940 + 615 + 1,185 + 395 - 4,275 = 39,990. Ignoring the balances gives 39,135.

stem: The bank balance was US\$1,890 at 1 January and US\$2,740 at 31 December. Total receipts were US\$52,310 and payments for business expenses and purchases were US\$44,865. All other withdrawals were the owner's drawings. Calculate the drawings.
hints: Opening balance + receipts - payments - drawings = closing balance.

stem: Thieves broke into Rudo's electrical shop and stole all the inventory except goods worth US\$1,950. Inventory at the start of the year was US\$12,480; purchases to the date were US\$47,150 and returns outwards US\$630. Sales to the date were US\$68,000 with no returns, and the usual gross profit margin is 30%. Calculate the value of inventory stolen.
hints: Cost of sales is 70% of sales.
Inventory before the theft = opening + net purchases - cost of sales.

stem: A wholesaler adds a mark-up of 60% to the cost of goods. Calculate the gross profit margin as a percentage of revenue, to one decimal place.
explanation: Cost 100, selling price 160, profit 60. Margin = 60 ÷ 160 × 100 = 37.5%. Giving 60% confuses mark-up with margin.
workedSolution: 1. Cost 100, selling price 160, profit 60. Margin = 60 ÷ 160 × 100 = 37.5%. Giving 60% confuses mark-up with margin.
hints: Take cost as 100: selling price is 160.

stem: Explain why a figure for cash stolen found as a balancing figure may be unreliable.

points.description: It absorbs every unrecorded or mistaken item, not only theft
Errors in takings, expenses paid from the till or banking would be included in it
Without records the owner cannot show the police or insurer that a theft occurred

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The figure is whatever is left after all known items, so any unrecorded expense or error is hidden in it. It does not prove theft. With no till records the owner cannot support a claim.

explanation: One mark for each reason.
hints: What else could the balancing figure contain?

stem: State two assumptions made when inventory lost in a fire is estimated using the gross profit margin.

points.description: The margin earned in the period before the fire was the same as the usual margin
The records of opening inventory, purchases and sales are complete and accurate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The margin was constant during the period and the opening inventory, purchases and sales records are complete.

explanation: One mark for each assumption.
hints: Think of the margin and of the records used.

stem: A shopkeeper pays all takings into the bank and pays wages and rent by cheque but keeps no cash book. Advise him on the records he should keep and evaluate the benefit.

points.description: Keep a cash book and ledgers so that sales, purchases and expenses are recorded separately
A trial balance then checks the accuracy and errors can be traced
Management can see sales, margins and expenses each month and control the business
Cost: time and possibly an accountant, but banks and ZIMRA require reliable records, so the benefits outweigh the cost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He should keep a cash book and ledger accounts. This gives separate figures for sales and expenses and a trial balance to check accuracy, so he can control costs and show lenders reliable statements. The time and cost are worth it for a growing business.

explanation: One mark for each reasoned point.
hints: What do full records give that totals do not?

stem:
A fire destroyed most of the inventory of Chipo's furniture shop in Gweru. The records show: inventory at 1 January US\$21,735; purchases to the date of the fire US\$69,480; returns outwards US\$1,185; sales to the date of the fire US\$96,320 (including cash sales); returns inwards US\$1,640. The business sells at a mark-up of 40% on cost. Salvaged goods are worth US\$3,150.

Trade receivables were US\$5,870 at 1 January and US\$6,385 on the date of the fire. Customers paid US\$71,465; discount allowed US\$940; irrecoverable debts US\$610.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of sales to the date of the fire (revenue = sales less returns inwards).
parts.explanation: Revenue 94,680; cost = revenue ÷ 1.40 = 67,628.57. Using 60% as if it were a margin gives 56,808.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Revenue 94,680; cost = revenue ÷ 1.40 = 67,628.57. Using 60% as if it were a margin gives 56,808.

parts.stem: The insurer questions the claim. Explain two reasons why the estimate might be wrong.

points.description: The mark-up may have varied, for example if goods were sold at a discount, so cost of sales and inventory would differ
Records of purchases, sales or returns may be incomplete or inaccurate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: If some goods were sold at a lower mark-up the estimated cost of sales is wrong. The calculation also relies on complete records of purchases, sales and returns.
